title: How Hot Air Balloons Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how hot air balloons work, starting with a bit of banter about Jules Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days and a Callaway Gardens balloon festival. They cover the history from the 1783 Montgolfier brothers' sheep, duck and rooster flight and the first human flights by Pilâtre de Rozier and the Marquis d'Arlandes, through smoke balloon carnival acts, the 1950s Navy-funded Raven Industries designs and the light-bulb envelope shape. They then explain the science of buoyancy and warm air being less dense, the envelope, nylon gores, propane burners and wicker baskets, piloting by altitude to find wind directions, ground crews, landing and champagne traditions, safety statistics, costs, and some balloon trivia. The episode ends with a listener mail about left-handed athletes like Rafael Nadal and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about Jules Verne's Around the World in Eighty Days and its balloon movie version, Josh's disinterest in riding a balloon, and a Callaway Gardens balloon festival.
topics: Around the World in Eighty Days

segments.title: Montgolfier brothers and first flights
segments.summary: The history begins with the 1783 Montgolfier brothers, their paper-company background, the sheep, duck, and rooster test flight before King Louis XVI, and the first human flight with the Marquis d'Arlandes and Pilâtre de Rozier, who later died in a hydrogen-hot air balloon attempt crossing the English Channel.

segments.title: Smoke balloons and the Flying Allens
segments.summary: Smoke balloon carnival acts in the late 1800s and early 1900s are described, including the Flying Allens family performing stunts under balloons.

segments.title: 1950s revival and modern design
segments.summary: Hot air balloons were revived in the 1950s after Navy interest; Ed Yost and Raven Industries developed the light-bulb envelope shape, and civilian sales began in the 1960s.

segments.title: Science of buoyancy
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh explain that warm air is less dense and rises, that heating air lifts roughly seven grams per cubic foot, and that the balloon works through buoyancy in the same way as a cork in water.

segments.title: Balloon parts: envelope, burner, basket
segments.summary: The envelope is made of nylon gores, the burners use liquid propane converted to gas at the burner, a quieter setting is available for livestock, the skirt is fire resistant, and wicker baskets absorb landing impact.

segments.title: Piloting, wind, and landing
segments.summary: Pilots control altitude with the burner and the deflation valve to pick wind layers that move them horizontally. They discuss power line hazards, weather checks, chase crews, setup and landing, and the champagne toast and balloonist blessing.

segments.title: Safety, costs, and festivals
segments.summary: Accident statistics from 1964 to 2014 are given, along with the Egypt fire, the cost of owning a balloon, novelty shapes, and the Callaway Gardens and Albuquerque festivals.

segments.title: Balloon trivia
segments.summary: Mental Floss trivia includes an 1808 French balloon duel and the Union Army balloon corps under Abraham Lincoln, which had balloons that a Confederate balloon was captured by.

segments.title: Listener mail: left-handedness in sports
segments.summary: A listener from Essex writes about Rafael Nadal being trained to play tennis left-handed, and whether dominant hand can be retrained.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts list ways to contact the show and sign off.
